## Santa Prisca Church in Taxco: architecture of a silver-mining town

The two tall towers of Santa Prisca Church rise above the white houses of [Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/) in the Mexican state of Guerrero. The church stands beside the town's main square, so you can admire its carved façade up close or see it from the upper neighborhoods, which offer panoramas of the densely built hillsides.

The church's full name is **Santa Prisca and San Sebastián**. It is one of the most recognizable examples of 18th-century Mexican Baroque architecture. Its construction is closely tied to silver mining, which brought Taxco fame and wealth.

## José de la Borda and the church's construction

The main patron of this ambitious project was José de la Borda, a wealthy businessman associated with silver mines. According to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), the reconstruction and creation of the new architectural complex took place in **1751–1758**. The work is associated with architect Pedro Durán and craftsman Juan Caballero.

Santa Prisca shows how income from precious-metal mining was transformed into monumental religious art. Unlike buildings connected with New Spain's administrative history, here the emphasis is on elaborate stone carving, sculpture and decoration.

## What to notice outside and inside

### Two towers and a carved façade

The façade is richly decorated. The **Churrigueresque** style, characteristic of late Spanish and New Spanish Baroque, is recognizable by its intricate carving, densely packed ornament and wealth of detail. View the façade from several distances: up close you can appreciate the stonecutters' skill, while the opposite side of the square reveals the overall composition of the two towers.

### Gilded altarpieces and paintings

Inside are richly decorated, gilded wooden retablos and paintings. INAH particularly highlights works by Miguel Cabrera, an important 18th-century New Spanish painter. If the interior is open, take time to study the main altar and side compositions. Remember that this is an active church: follow visiting rules and avoid disturbing services.

Santa Prisca is particularly interesting if you have already seen Mexico's early monasteries. A comparison with the more restrained [Cuernavaca Cathedral complex](/mexico/place/cuernavaca-cathedral/) shows how religious architecture and ecclesiastical decoration evolved over two centuries.

## Including Santa Prisca in your journey

The church is in central Taxco, where the surrounding streets climb the hillsides. Comfortable shoes are useful: changes in elevation are noticeable even over short distances. Combine a visit with the main square, silver workshops and views of the historic town.

On our [religious journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), you can visit Santa Prisca along with other churches and monuments. For the town's history, silver craftsmanship and comparisons between itineraries, consult the [Taxco guide](/mexico/place/taxco/) and [Mexico's culture and history tours](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/).

The church is still in use. If viewing the interior is your main goal, check opening arrangements, liturgical services and possible restoration restrictions in advance. Timetables and photography rules may change.

## Frequently asked questions about Santa Prisca Church

### In which century was Santa Prisca built?

In the 18th century. The main construction campaign took place from 1751 to 1758, when Taxco was closely associated with silver mining.

### Who paid for construction?

The principal commissioner and patron was José de la Borda, whose wealth came from silver mines.

### What makes the church architecturally famous?

Its two richly decorated towers, Churrigueresque carved façade and gilded interior altarpieces.

### Where is Santa Prisca Church?

In the historic center of [Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/), beside the main square. You can see the church from the streets and viewpoints of this hillside town.

## Which tour includes Santa Prisca Church in Taxco?

[Santa Prisca Church](/mexico/place/santa-prisca-taxco/) stands in the center of hillside [Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/), a town in the state of Guerrero that grew wealthy through silver mining. Visitors come for its Baroque façade, carved altarpieces and continuing Catholic tradition. On a journey through central Mexico, though, the context also matters: is this a brief architectural stop or a complete pilgrimage service?

Our collection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} in which Santa Prisca is on the **main itinerary** and is included in the program. Five Holy Masses are scheduled in different churches; one is held at Santa Prisca on **April 5**. Participants spend all 6 nights in Mexico City, so this tour does not include an overnight stay in Taxco.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_mexico_religious_journey}}

## How the day visiting Santa Prisca unfolds

**April 5, day five of the journey.** After breakfast, the group departs Mexico City for [Cuernavaca](/mexico/place/cuernavaca/). Visits to the Palace of Cortés and the cathedral are planned here, followed by a drive to Taxco. In the historic center, the group visits Santa Prisca for Mass, then returns to Mexico City for dinner and the night.

This arrangement introduces two very different cities in central Mexico in one day. Cuernavaca presents early colonial architecture, while Taxco reveals silver-mining history and church Baroque. There is a road transfer between the cities, and time for independent walks depends on the excursion schedule. Spending a full day in Taxco, visiting workshops and staying overnight would require a different itinerary to be arranged separately.

Details of these visits also appear in the stand-alone [Cuernavaca, Taxco and Mass at Santa Prisca excursion](/mexico/cuernavaca/cuernavaca-taxco-pilgrimage/), which is part of the pilgrimage tour and sets out the day's combined stops.

## Why Santa Prisca deserves special attention

The church's main façade faces Taxco's historic square, while two ornamented towers rise above the town's white houses. They are visible against the hills and serve as landmarks when walking the old streets.

Construction was financed by silver entrepreneur **José de la Borda**, who supported the renewal of the parish church in the 18th century. In Taxco this commemorates an era when silver mining shaped the town's prosperity. Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) notes the significance of the decorative altarpieces, painting and richly furnished interior. The façade is only part of the experience: inside are gilded carving, religious paintings and details typical of Mexican Baroque.

Santa Prisca remains an active place of worship. During Mass, pilgrimage participants come primarily for the service; any interior sightseeing must respect the religious life of the parish. Current visiting rules determine opening hours, photography and freedom of movement inside.

## How this tour differs from an ordinary Taxco excursion

Simply seeing a town name on a route does not explain why it is visited. In the [general collection of tours through Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/tour/), you can compare the pilgrimage with broader Mexico journeys where Taxco is a stop between colonial towns and the Pacific coast.

| Criterion | Pilgrimage itinerary |
|---|---|
| Main purpose | Holy Mass at Santa Prisca |
| Visit date | April 5, 2027 |
| Visited alongside Taxco | Cuernavaca |
| Overnight stay | Return to Mexico City |
| Entire journey | 7 days, 6 nights |

If churches, shrines and religious services are your priorities, the religious journey directly addresses them. If you prefer Taxco's silver workshops, colonial streets and free time, choose based on the length of the stop rather than Santa Prisca simply appearing on a list.

## How the pilgrimage through central Mexico is organized

Santa Prisca is one of 5 places where Mass is celebrated during the journey. The route begins in Mexico City, visiting the [Shrine of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/) and the historic center with [Santo Domingo Church](/mexico/place/santo-domingo-mexico-city/). Another day is devoted to Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla. After Taxco, the itinerary visits [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco. This sequence connects the pilgrimage with the history and culture of central Mexico.

The [seven-day program](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) includes **private transfers and excursions**, an English-speaking guide, 6 nights at Casa Blanca 4* or a hotel of a similar category, breakfasts and dinners according to the schedule, admission to listed attractions and 5 Masses. A minibus is specified for groups of up to 24 people; a touring coach is used for 25 or more. Airfares and drinks are among the exclusions.

The hotel acts as one base throughout the journey. After a busy day in Cuernavaca and Taxco, guests return to the same accommodation without having to change hotels for a single church visit. This suits organized pilgrim groups wishing to stay at one address in the capital.

## Preparing for the trip to Taxco

Taxco is hilly, with historic streets that can be steep, cobbled and stepped. For Santa Prisca, choose non-slip shoes and clothing suitable for worship. Participants who find hills difficult should discuss walking distances and vehicle drop-off points near the center in advance.

The excursion day includes travel from Mexico City, stops in Cuernavaca, a visit to Taxco and the return drive. When planning extra activities, remember this sequence: time for silver shops or a long photo walk is not automatically included. Ada Tours can help coordinate the group's pace and order of stops to reflect the itinerary and participants' religious interests.

## Frequently asked questions about tours visiting Santa Prisca

### Can I visit Santa Prisca on a current Ada Tours trip?

Yes. The church is included in the [seven-day pilgrimage](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), with Mass scheduled on April 5, 2027. The catalog includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring this place on the main itinerary.

### Is an overnight stay in Taxco included?

No. Under the current program, guests return to Mexico City after Cuernavaca and Taxco. All 6 nights are in the capital.

### Is this an exclusively religious trip?

The focus is Catholic pilgrimage with 5 Masses, but the itinerary also includes historic monuments, museums and [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/). The order of services and excursions follows the agreed program.

### Can this be considered a stand-alone Taxco tour?

No. Santa Prisca is visited during part of one day within a seven-day route through central Mexico. For a longer stay in the town, compare [other tours through Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/tour/) and their accommodation.

### Is there a fixed price just for visiting Santa Prisca?

The published program has no separate price for this stop. The excursion and Mass are part of the overall pilgrimage; the services and conditions are listed on the [tour page](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/).

## Santo Domingo Church in Mexico City: Baroque and Dominican history

Santo Domingo Church (Templo de Santo Domingo) stands north of the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/) in Mexico City's historic center. It is an active Catholic church with a striking dark-red stone façade, a carved portal and a tall bell tower. It is worth including in an itinerary for anyone interested in colonial architecture, religious painting and the old city's history.

Dominican friars arrived in Mexico City soon after the Spanish conquest. The first church on the site dates to the 16th century, but the present structure largely took shape in the 18th. The complex has survived floods, rebuilding and changes to the city layout over the centuries.

## What to see on the façade and inside the church

From the square, the contrast between the reddish walls and lighter carved features of the portal is clear. The tower rises above neighboring buildings, but there is more to discover beyond the entrance.

Inside are **gilded Baroque altarpieces**, paintings, sculptures and side chapels. Venerated images include Our Lady of the Rosary and Our Lady of Covadonga, to whom one of the large 18th-century altars is dedicated.

Notice how the light changes the appearance of the carving and gilding. The richly detailed decoration is characteristic of New Spanish Baroque, yet this remains a living religious space, used for prayer and Mass.

When a service is taking place, explore the interior discreetly. Access to particular altars and side areas may depend on the church schedule.

## Why so little remains of the large monastery

The story of Santo Domingo begins with a 16th-century Dominican monastery. It once occupied a much larger area than the present church. Its buildings served the community's daily life, education and religious work.

In the 19th century, reforms and redevelopment changed land ownership, and parts of the complex and several chapels were lost. The construction of a new street divided the historic space. The church now appears to be a stand-alone monument, although it originally belonged to a large complex.

The surrounding square and streets show how Mexico City's colonial environment evolved along with the administrative and civic life of the capital.

## Santo Domingo Square: what is nearby?

Santo Domingo Square developed alongside the monastery in the colonial period. Interesting buildings in the ensemble include the old customs house, former viceregal institutions and historic arcades associated with the work of scribes. The tradition of asking public scribes to prepare documents is part of the area's memory.

From here, it is easy to continue to [Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/) and the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/). To explore connections between religious and state authority, add the [National Palace](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/) or [Old Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/).

Within this compact historic district you can encounter several stories: a monastic order, the city's central square and the principal institutions of colonial Mexico City.

## Do not confuse it with Santo Domingo in Puebla

Several well-known churches in Mexico are dedicated to Saint Dominic. Travelers should distinguish **Santo Domingo in Mexico City** from [Santo Domingo and its Rosary Chapel in Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/). They are in different cities, although both share Dominican heritage.

The Puebla church is especially famous for its lavish Rosary Chapel; the capital's church has different interiors, altars and history. They are separate stops on an itinerary, not different names for the same place.

## Including Santo Domingo in your visit

Allow roughly **30–60 minutes** to see the façade, square and accessible interiors. More time is needed for architectural details and neighboring buildings. Photography and visiting during services are subject to the church's rules.

We include Santo Domingo in the [seven-day Religious Journey Through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), where capital-city shrines are combined with visits to Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla. To explore the center independently, begin at the Zócalo, walk to Santo Domingo and then return to the cathedral.

## Frequently asked questions about Santo Domingo Church

### Where is Santo Domingo Church located?

In Mexico City's historic center, beside Santo Domingo Square north of the Zócalo. It can be included in a walking route through the center.

### Can visitors go inside?

It is an active church, but access depends on services and current arrangements. Check opening hours before planning a special visit.

### What makes it interesting beyond the façade?

Its Baroque altars and chapels, religious images and the history of the large Dominican monastery, much of which has been lost.

### Is this the same church as the one in Puebla?

No. [Santo Domingo Church and the Rosary Chapel in Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/) form a separate monument in another city.

### What can I combine with a visit?

A walk around the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/) and [Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), which reveal different aspects of the capital's colonial history.

## Which tour visits Santo Domingo in Mexico City?

[Santo Domingo Church](/mexico/place/santo-domingo-mexico-city/) stands on its namesake square in Mexico City's historic center. Visitors come for its Dominican history, Baroque decoration and religious services. Our collection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} in which this church is a required part of the journey.

On the current [seven-day Religious Journey Through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), Santo Domingo is visited on **April 3, 2027**. The pilgrimage runs from April 1 to 7 and includes **5 Holy Masses in different churches**. One takes place in Santo Domingo, with the others held at shrines across central Mexico. All 6 nights are spent in Mexico City.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_mexico_religious_journey}}

## April 3 itinerary: from the Zócalo to Garibaldi

After breakfast, travelers head to the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), the capital's main square. The next stop is Santo Domingo Church, where Mass is scheduled. The group then continues exploring the old city, visiting [Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), the [National Palace](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/) and the [former Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/).

The second part of the day takes guests to [Garibaldi Square](/mexico/place/garibaldi-plaza/), famous for its mariachi tradition. After the walk, the group returns to its Mexico City hotel for dinner and the night. The day combines prayer, religious architecture, the capital's history and music.

The full sequence appears in the separate [Mexico City Churches, Mass and Garibaldi Square excursion](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/). **Visiting the National Palace depends on access rules.** During official events, some rooms, including those containing murals, may be closed. Entry to its interior must not be regarded as guaranteed when the palace is closed.

## Why Santo Domingo Church is worth visiting

The Dominicans arrived in Mexico City in the 16th century. Their monastery and church underwent several rebuildings. The present church mostly dates to the 18th century and faces the historic square. It has reddish stone, a carved portal and a tall bell tower.

Altarpieces and sacred images survive inside. The church is associated with devotion to Our Lady of the Rosary and Our Lady of Covadonga. For pilgrims it is above all a place of prayer; for those interested in history, it shows how religious orders helped shape the colonial capital.

[Santo Domingo Square](/mexico/place/santo-domingo-mexico-city/) also deserves attention. Historically it contained church and city administrative buildings, while scribes known as "evangelistas" worked under the arcades, helping people prepare documents and letters. Mexico's INAH recognizes the square and church as part of the capital's historic heritage.

## Distinguishing Santo Domingo from the church in Puebla

Santo Domingo appears twice on the pilgrimage itinerary, but these are **two separate churches**. The one in Mexico City is visited on April 3. The following day the group travels to Tlaxcala and Puebla, where it visits [another Santo Domingo with the Rosary Chapel](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/).

| Place | Program day |
|---|---|
| Santo Domingo, Mexico City | April 3, Mass |
| Santo Domingo, Puebla | April 4, excursion |
| Santa Prisca, Taxco | April 5, Mass |

This distinction is essential when choosing the trip. The [Santa Prisca day](/mexico/place/santa-prisca-taxco/tour/) also includes Cuernavaca and a return to Mexico City. The day in the capital focuses on the Zócalo, churches, palaces and Garibaldi. Similar church names do not make these stops interchangeable.

## What is included in the pilgrimage week?

The seven-day program confirms **private transfers and excursions**, an English-speaking guide, 6 nights at Casa Blanca 4* or a hotel of a similar standard, scheduled breakfasts and dinners, entrance tickets to listed attractions and 5 Holy Masses. Groups of up to 24 guests use a minibus; those with 25 or more use a touring coach. Airfares and personal expenses are excluded.

Staying at one Mexico City hotel means guests need not pack their luggage after every day trip. The group visits shrines and monuments during the day and returns to the capital in the evening. This suits pilgrimage communities that want a known order of services and one accommodation address.

The route includes both the [Shrine of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/) and [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/). It combines Catholic traditions with Mexican history, but it is not a flexible, independent holiday with an unrestricted schedule.

## Practical visiting arrangements: what to agree on beforehand

In an active church, the group's primary purpose is worship. Time inside and access to individual areas depend on the parish's current arrangements. Modest attire is appropriate for Mass; photography and movement through the church during a service should be agreed locally.

The day includes walking around Mexico City's historic center. Travelers who struggle with longer walks should discuss the distance, vehicle drop-off points and order of stops in advance. Ada Tours can coordinate the group's pace and transfers within the confirmed itinerary. Guiding in other languages, extra stops and changes to the day's duration require separate agreement: this program includes an English-speaking guide.

## Frequently asked questions

### On which day is Mass held at Santo Domingo?

**April 3, 2027**, on the third day of the [Mexico religious tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/). It is one of the 5 Masses included.

### Can Santo Domingo and the Metropolitan Cathedral be visited together?

Yes. [The Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/) and Santo Domingo Church appear on the same sightseeing day in central Mexico City. They are separate churches.

### Why are access restrictions mentioned for the National Palace?

It is a protected government property, and entry depends on official events. Some rooms and murals may not be accessible to visitors.

### Is a transfer to a hotel in another city included?

No. All 6 nights are spent in Mexico City, including the night after the Santo Domingo excursion.

### Is Santo Domingo in Puebla also included in this trip?

Yes, but it is a [different church in Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/), visited on the following day, April 4.

## Sumidero Canyon: boat rides and viewpoints in Chiapas

**Sumidero Canyon (Cañón del Sumidero)** is a natural gorge on the Grijalva River in the Mexican state of **Chiapas**. Its vertical walls look particularly imposing from the water as boats pass between cliffs and plants cling to ledges and cracks. In some sections the walls are hundreds of meters high, reaching approximately a kilometer.

The canyon is within a **national park** protecting the landscape, river and local wildlife. Two main visiting formats are available: an organized boat tour or land-based viewpoints high above the water. They offer different experiences, transportation needs and restrictions.

For a journey through Chiapas, Sumidero works well as a separate nature stop near **Tuxtla Gutiérrez** and **Chiapa de Corzo**. The route may then continue toward the region's mountain towns, but those transfers must be planned separately.

## Cruising the Grijalva River: what happens on the route?

The best-known way to experience the canyon is **by motorboat along the Grijalva River**. Trips depart from **Chiapa de Corzo** and neighboring piers served by authorized operators. From the water, the rock faces rise almost vertically, and the shoreline changes from green slopes to tall limestone walls.

On the boat you can see striking rock formations, vegetation and birds. The itinerary depends on current navigation permissions, water levels and safety conditions. Do not assume every boat follows exactly the same path or visits every site mentioned in older guidebooks.

### Natural features along the way

The canyon contains remarkable rock shapes, small waterfalls and geological forms, including a famous plant-covered formation known as the **Christmas Tree (Árbol de Navidad)**. Its appearance is closely tied to moisture and seasonal water flow.

Birds inhabit the national park, and **river crocodiles** can be seen near the water in some areas. Mexico's conservation service also lists spider monkeys among the park's species. The presence of animals in the ecosystem does not mean they will be spotted on every boat excursion.

Do not approach wild animals too closely or try to feed them. Photographing wildlife from the water must remain observation, not interference with the animals' behavior.

### Boat safety

Choose a boat operator working under current regulations. Wear a **life jacket** and follow the captain's instructions throughout the journey. Do not stand while the boat is moving at speed or lean over the side for photographs.

Boat traffic in Sumidero Canyon can be restricted for safety. CONANP has documented temporary closures of sections following rockfalls and slope inspections. This is why visitors should confirm availability immediately before departure rather than assuming a permanent schedule.

## Land-based viewpoints

Another way to see the canyon is to drive to the **miradores**, viewpoints on the high rim. From above, the gorge has a different geometry, revealing bends in the river, cliff edges and forested hills.

The viewpoints follow a road route from the Tuxtla Gutiérrez side. It is best to plan them separately, particularly if you are also taking a long boat excursion. Driving between stops and allowing time at each can take a significant part of the day.

The advantage is broad panoramic photography and a sense of the gorge's depth without going aboard a boat. However, access to each viewpoint, safety barriers and opening hours must be checked against current national park notices.

| Format | Main experience |
|---|---|
| Motorboat on the Grijalva | Seeing cliffs from below |
| Viewpoints | Panorama from above |
| Both formats | A full day of nature |
| Wildlife watching | Depends on chance |

## Where is the canyon and how do you reach it?

For boat trips, visitors commonly depart from **Chiapa de Corzo**, a separate town near Tuxtla Gutiérrez. Travelers staying in **San Cristóbal de las Casas** can include Sumidero in a Chiapas itinerary, but should account for actual outward and return travel time.

Avoid trying to combine a drive from a mountain town, a lengthy boat trip, every viewpoint and other excursions in an unrealistically short day. If you want both visiting formats, set priorities in advance.

On a wider [Mexico](/mexico/) journey, the canyon can complement the archaeological sites at [Palenque](/mexico/place/palenque/). These are different parts of Chiapas, however, requiring a separate route and time on the road.

## Seasons and the best time to visit

Chiapas is generally rainier **from May through October**, with drier months usually falling in late autumn, winter and early spring. Waterfalls and greenery change in appearance with rainfall. Heavy rain may also restrict boat trips because of visibility, water levels or rockfall risks.

A morning departure is often convenient for the boat trip, leaving some margin for schedule changes. On an open boat, allow for sun and wind; take a hat, water and protection for cameras against spray. Closed-toe shoes and sun protection are useful at viewpoints.

In the national park, follow the regulations, stay on designated paths and keep away from cliff edges outside protected areas. Even a beautiful view is not worth the risk of an unsafe photograph.

## Including Sumidero in a journey

Sumidero Canyon is an appealing nature stop on a Chiapas itinerary when you want to see a river, mountains and wild slopes after exploring towns. Travelers interested in canyons, rivers and mountain panoramas can browse the [Nature theme](/interests/nature/). Possible animal encounters during a boat ride do not make it a dedicated safari. Check the chosen tour's description for the actual boat itinerary, its duration and whether tickets are included.

Compare all current Mexico programs in our [Mexico tours catalog](/mexico/tour/). Simply seeing Chiapas or Tuxtla Gutiérrez mentioned in a route does not guarantee that the canyon is included.

## Frequently asked questions about Sumidero Canyon

### Where is Sumidero Canyon?

In Chiapas, southern Mexico, on the Grijalva River near Tuxtla Gutiérrez and Chiapa de Corzo.

### Which is better: a boat or viewpoints?

The boat reveals the cliffs from below, while viewpoints provide a broad panorama from above. If you have time for only one, choose according to whether you prefer a boat ride or panoramic views.

### Can you see crocodiles?

Crocodiles inhabit the national park ecosystem, but sightings on a particular excursion are not guaranteed. Observe them from a safe distance.

### Can navigation be closed?

Yes. Authorities may restrict boat traffic due to weather, rockfalls and other risks. Check availability before traveling.

### Is the canyon suitable for families with children?

An organized trip is possible when the operator's requirements are met, appropriate life jackets are available and passengers behave safely aboard. Check age restrictions and other conditions with the operator.
